Plenary Inspiration
PLEE-nuh-ree in-SPIH-ray-shun
noun phrase (doctrine of Scripture)
Latin plenus (full, complete, entire) + English inspiration, from Latin inspiratio (a breathing into, from in + spirare, to breathe); the compound doctrine that the divine inspiration of Scripture extends to the whole of each book and to every part of the whole — not merely to the spiritually significant portions or to the doctrinal core — so that every verse, every chapter, every book of the 66-book Protestant canon is equally breathed out by God

Biblical Definition

Plenary inspiration is the doctrine that God's authoritative speaking extends to the whole of Scripture without remainder. The Greek theopneustos of 2 Timothy 3:16 — “breathed out by God” — is applied to “all Scripture,” not to selected portions. The adjective “all” (pasa) carries the doctrinal weight: it forecloses the move of accepting the doctrinal core while treating historical narrations, genealogies, or apocalyptic details as uninspired. 2 Peter 1:21 grounds the mechanism: “men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit” — the same Spirit who superintended the prophets' inspired speech operated throughout the entire text they produced. Matthew 5:18 reinforces the scope: not even the smallest letter or stroke shall pass from the Law. Christ's hermeneutic applies the whole Law as authoritative, not merely its ethical core. Plenary inspiration does not dissolve the human authors into divine dictation machines; the full personality, vocabulary, literary style, and historical situation of each human author is employed by the Spirit. But the Spirit's superintendence ensures that what the human authors wrote is also precisely what God breathed out, extending to the whole without exception. The result is a Scripture that is fully human in form and fully divine in authority across every part, profitable for teaching, reproof, correction, and training in righteousness (2 Tim 3:16).

Webster 1828 Definition

PLENARY INSPIRATION: the doctrine that divine inspiration extends to the whole of Scripture — every book, chapter, verse, and part of the 66-book Protestant canon — without restricting the Spirit's superintendence to doctrinal or spiritually significant portions; grounded in 2 Timothy 3:16 (“all Scripture is breathed out by God”) and partnered with verbal inspiration (every word) to form the classical doctrine of verbal-plenary inspiration.

PLENARY INSPIRATION. Noun phrase. The doctrine that God's authoritative breathing-out of Scripture extends to the entirety of the biblical text — all 66 books, every chapter, every verse — not merely to its religious or doctrinal core. Grounded in the Greek pasa (“all”) of 2 Timothy 3:16.

The complementary doctrine is verbal inspiration: the Spirit's superintendence extended not only to the whole (plenary) but to the very words (verbal). Together they form the classical doctrine of verbal-plenary inspiration, the standard formulation of Protestant evangelical orthodoxy from the Reformers through the Princeton theologians (Charles Hodge, B.B. Warfield) to the Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy (1978).

Plenary inspiration is not dictation: the human authors retained their own personality, vocabulary, historical horizon, literary style, and emotional register. The Spirit used all of these as instruments. But superintendence ensures that what the human authors wrote is precisely what God intended — so that the result is both fully human and fully authoritative as the word of God.

The doctrine stands against “partial inspiration” views: that inspiration extends only to matters of faith and practice (neo-orthodox), or only to the autographs' doctrinal core, or that the Spirit's direction of the human authors varies in degree from book to book. Against all partial views: “all Scripture is breathed out by God” (2 Tim 3:16) admits no portion as uninspired.

Key Scripture

2 Tim 3:16 — "All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:"

2 Pet 1:21 — "For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost."

Matt 5:18 — "For verily I say unto you, Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled."

Ps 19:7 — "The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul: the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple."

Modern Corruption

Neo-orthodox theology (Barth, Brunner) restricts inspiration to the spiritual encounter Scripture occasions rather than the text itself; liberal higher criticism limits authority to the “assured results” of historical-critical research, treating large portions of Scripture as uninspired human composition.

expand to see more

Karl Barth and Emil Brunner distinguished sharply between the Word of God (Christ, the living self-disclosure of God) and the words of Scripture (a human fallible witness to that disclosure). For Barth, Scripture “becomes” the Word of God in the existential event of the Spirit's work in the reader — it is not intrinsically and objectively God's word across its entirety. Brunner went further, insisting that the doctrine of verbal-plenary inspiration involves an error-theory that contradicts the Spirit's activity through fallible human instruments. On both accounts, the pasa of 2 Timothy 3:16 is reinterpreted: “all Scripture” becomes “Scripture where it occasions genuine encounter with God,” which excludes the genealogies, the historical narrations, and the portions higher criticism regards as legendary or myth-laden.

Liberal Protestant higher criticism produced a graduated theory of inspiration: some texts of Scripture are “more inspired” because they contribute to the progressive development of Israel's religion toward its apex in the ethical monotheism of the Hebrew prophets and the Sermon on the Mount. The rest — the imprecatory Psalms, the Mosaic legislation including its sacrificial system, the apocalyptic imagery of Revelation — is the human vessel that the developing Spirit of God had not yet fully refined. The result is a Scripture whose authority is distributed unevenly according to the reader's judgment of its moral and theological development, with the human critic sitting in judgment over which portions God actually breathed out. This is the direct reversal of the doctrine: not “all Scripture” but “the Scripture I judge spiritually worthy.”

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin plenus (full, complete) + inspiration from Latin inspirare (to breathe into); the Greek doctrinal ground is theopneustos (2 Tim 3:16, God-breathed) applied to pasa graphē (all Scripture); the compound doctrine verbal-plenary inspiration was given systematic form by Charles Hodge, A.A. Hodge, and B.B. Warfield at Princeton in the 19th century.

expand to see more

Greek theopneustos (θεοπνευστοζ) — “God-breathed”; compound of theos (God) + pneō (to breathe); 2 Timothy 3:16 applies this term to “all Scripture” (pasa graphē); the image is divine outbreathing rather than divine inbreathing into human authors — Scripture is what God breathed out

Latin plenus — full, complete, entire; the Latin church father Augustine applied it to the canon in the sense that no portion of Scripture falls outside divine superintendence; in 19th-century Princeton theology it became the technical term for the scope of inspiration (the whole) as distinct from the mode (verbal) and the result (inerrancy)

Charles Hodge (1797–1878) and B.B. Warfield (1851–1921) — Princeton theologians who gave the doctrine “verbal-plenary inspiration” its classic systematic form; Warfield's essay “Inspiration” in The International Standard Bible Encyclopaedia (1915) remains the standard Reformed treatment

Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy (1978) — the ecumenical evangelical formulation that affirmed verbal-plenary inspiration: “We affirm that inspiration, strictly speaking, applies only to the autographic text of Scripture, which in the providence of God can be ascertained from available manuscripts with great accuracy”; the Affirmations and Denials in Article VIII explicitly reject limited or partial inspiration

1689 LBCF 1.2 — the confessional basis: “Under the name of Holy Scripture, or the Word of God written, are now contained all the books of the Old and New Testament” — all 66, without graduation; confessional authority attaches to the whole canon equally, the practical application of plenary inspiration

Usage

"Preaching doctrine about Scripture must resist the appeal to a “canon within the canon” — a favorite of both liberal and evangelical pragmatists, who privilege certain books (Paul, the Synoptics) and treat the rest as less authoritative. The plenary doctrine rules out this hierarchy: God breathed out all Scripture, and the preacher's job is to preach all of it, including the portions contemporary hearers find difficult (the imprecatory Psalms, the Mosaic laws, the apocalyptic visions). The difficulty of a text is not evidence of its uninspiredness."

"Apologetically, the plenary doctrine is the necessary ground of inerrancy: if the Spirit's superintendence extends to the whole of Scripture, then an error in any portion of Scripture would be an error in a portion God breathed out — which contradicts the character of the God who cannot lie (Tit 1:2). The plenary doctrine provides the logical foundation for the inerrancy claim; inerrancy that applies only to “faith and practice” topics is simply a restatement of partial inspiration under a different name."

"The genealogies of Matthew 1 and Luke 3 are test cases for the plenary doctrine. Liberal and neo-orthodox interpreters treat them as expendable filler, not inspired in any meaningful sense. The plenary doctrine insists otherwise: Christ's documented legal and biological descent from Abraham and David (Matt 1) and from Adam (Luke 3) grounds claims the New Testament makes about His fulfillment of covenant and His federal headship of a new humanity. The genealogies are not exhaustive history; they are theologically selected, and the Spirit breathed them out for the profitable purposes 2 Timothy 3:16 names."
